Title: Five Findings From the 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
Context: When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program...
Full Text:
The much anticipated State of Threat Intelligence report has just been published. The State of Threat Intelligence report is based on a survey Recorded Future conducted with UserEvidence of 768 cybersecurity professionals at enterprises with at least 1,000 employees. It’s the latest edition in our annual report series, where we gauge how threat intelligence is currently being used, funded, and measured. When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program and is planning for the year ahead. Here are my top five findings and why.

1. Cost is the least common reason to consolidate

A strong majority of respondents (79%) said they plan to consolidate threat intelligence vendors in the next year. That alone is no huge surprise, especially given that respondents reported using an average of five different vendors. Cost would be a reasonable guess for why, but reducing costs actually ranked last of five drivers, at 5%.

The drivers that ranked higher point to what teams want from consolidation:

Improving correlation across signals (34%): connecting intelligence across threat domains and internal telemetry into one view of risk.

Bringing siloed tools together (29%): ensuring different risk owners can efficiently act on intelligence.

Simplifying operations (22%): fewer interfaces and handoffs so teams can act on intelligence sooner.

Reducing vendor-management overhead (9%): fewer vendors to evaluate and renew.

Overall investment is still rising: 83% plan to increase threat intelligence spending in the next 12 months. Teams are consolidating to get better results from their intelligence, not to cut spend.

That puts the focus on outcomes. Jason Steer, CISO at Recorded Future, framed the risk well: consolidation only counts “if that provider has the same or better outcomes.” For anyone evaluating vendors this year, that’s the bar to consider.

Especially as teams expand the reach of their threat intelligence programs and support more stakeholders across the enterprise, they’re pursuing vendors that provide coverage across the risk domains that matter for those teams, but equally important that friction is not created in that pursuit of breadth, and that the organization is able to see how threats across disparate domains actually connect.

2. Only 25% have external intelligence and internal telemetry in one place

Correlation is the top consolidation driver, yet only a quarter of respondents say external intelligence and internal telemetry reside in one place. The rest break down as follows:

52% are partially integrated across some tools.

18% rely on manual correlation by analysts.

5% keep the two in separate workflows.

Poor integration with existing tools and workflows was also the most-cited pain point with current vendors.

This doesn’t mean every team needs to move everything into a single tool. What often matters is whether external intelligence can be correlated with internal signals across the tools a team already uses, without an analyst doing it by hand. Collective Insights® is built for this: it pulls detections from a team’s existing security tools and enriches them with Recorded Future intelligence.

For the 70% who are partially integrated or correlating manually, it’s worth identifying where that manual handoff still happens.

3. Confidence in ROI is high, but few measure cost savings

Nearly every respondent (99%) formally measures the value of their threat intelligence program, and 57% say they are very confident in their ability to quantify its ROI. But when asked how they measure value, more than half (58%) of that very confident group did not include cost savings. Across all respondents, 39% measure cost savings, and 31% measure whether triggered actions actually worked.

The most common metrics are operational:

Enhanced threat detection rates: 60%

Improved response times: 59%

Fewer incidents: 57%

Those matter to security teams, but ultimately fail to communicate the bottom-line impact of your threat intelligence program to the business. The Impact & Metrics dashboard in the Recorded Future platform helps here by showing the hours and dollars saved through use of the platform.

4. About one in four have already closed the loop

Closing that measurement gap depends on connecting intelligence to outcomes. That is what closed-loop operationalization does: intelligence is automatically shared with the relevant stakeholders, they take action based on it, and the efficacy of that action is validated and used to inform what intelligence is collected and shared with these teams.

Closed-loop programs can answer the questions stakeholders outside security ask: did the intelligence drive an action, and did that action work? Answering those questions also requires a clear definition of what intelligence should achieve. Most programs have that starting point: 68% say formally documented, regularly reviewed Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) govern their program.

For teams building next year’s measurement plan, PIRs set the benchmark, and closed-loop validation should be the goal for how outcomes get measured against it.

5. Threat intelligence is now an input to AI, not only a beneficiary of it

98% of respondents use AI in their threat intelligence work. Less discussed is the other direction: 74% say threat intelligence already feeds their organization’s AI or automation initiatives.

44% describe this as established, with intelligence regularly feeding one or more AI or automation workflows.

30% describe it as advanced, with structured intelligence as a core input across their AI and agentic systems.

Only 4% don’t use threat intelligence to support AI at all.

Across all of the tasks where we assessed comfort with AI autonomy (summarization, alert triage, enrichment, false-positive reduction, detection rule generation, prioritization, and enforcement actions), at least 92% of respondents are comfortable giving AI some role. That makes the earlier findings more pressing. AI workflows inherit whatever gaps exist in the intelligence they draw on, including signals that aren’t correlated and actions that aren’t validated.

Looking ahead

Taken together, these findings describe programs that are still investing. Their focus is on connecting intelligence, proving its value, and extending it into new workflows, including AI. Most are partway through that work, and some are further along than expected.

The full 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report covers each of these areas in more depth. That includes which teams beyond the SOC rely on threat intelligence and how comfortable organizations are giving AI autonomy. Download the report.

Title: AI Is Both Target and Tool for Threat Actors
Context: Summary Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier
Full Text:
Summary

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier. Of the 103 AI-enabled incidents analyzed for this report, most involve AI accelerating familiar attack types (supply-chain compromise, phishing, extortion) and making them more convincing. The use of AI is evident throughout the attack lifecycle, though full automation remains rare. Note: The period of analysis for this report is between July 31, 2025 and July 31, 2026.

Developer tools are a prime target. Because AI coding assistants and proxy packages often have privileged access to credentials and code, threat actors use them as footholds for mass credential theft and lateral movement across downstream environments.

State-sponsored actors are beginning to experiment with agentic capabilities. Most of the state-sponsored activity in this report falls within Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model Level 2–3 (AI-assisted malware development), with one notable exception: a campaign against Taiwanese government entities that employed up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.

Fully autonomous attacks remain rare, likely for both maturity and operational-risk reasons. Human oversight still appears necessary for reliable outcomes, which may limit the full automation of cyberattacks, especially in sensitive operations where an agent's error can have outsized consequences.

This restraint is unlikely to hold. As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising "noise" from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats.

Title: DoppelCart Fraud Network Grows to More Than 250,000 Domains
Context: According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled...
Full Text:
Summary

This article examines DoppelCart, a large-scale shopping fraud network encompassing approximately 261,700 suspected domains identified by Recorded Future. These fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ branding and product listings to deceive shoppers into disclosing personal and payment information, with some also capturing bank-issued verification codes to authorize fraudulent transactions. This research highlights the network’s widespread impersonation of US brands, evolving hosting infrastructure, and use of shared payment-routing configurations and the Medusa e-commerce platform. With approximately 40% of observed DoppelCart websites remaining active, understanding these patterns can help retailers identify brand impersonation and help consumers recognize fraudulent shopping sites.

Background

In September 2026, German cybersecurity company Nebty exposed DoppelCart, a large-scale online shopping fraud network with over 119,000 websites. The fraudulent storefronts copy legitimate retailers’ product listings, images, and descriptions to deceive shoppers into entering payment information.

Researchers identified shared website designs, code, and infrastructure across thousands of suspicious storefronts, eventually linking the domains to the DoppelCart cluster. Most websites used .shop web addresses, and many advertised steep discounts, including offers of 65% off, to attract shoppers. Although the websites shared technical characteristics, Nebty cautioned that the findings did not establish whether a single criminal organization operated the entire network.

According to subsequent reporting by Malwarebytes and BleepingComputer, fraudulent checkout pages transmit shoppers’ personal and payment information to attacker-controlled servers in real time. Some also capture one-time verification codes issued by banks, potentially allowing criminals to authorize transactions while victims believe they are completing legitimate purchases.

Domains Discovered by Recorded Future

Primarily between March and October 2026, Recorded Future used proprietary methods to identify approximately 261,700 unique apex domains that are likely part of the DoppelCart fraud network. Based on our collections, a few thousand DoppelCart detections began appearing in January 2026 and increased during March. Our detections peaked during the months of June and July, with a sharp drop-off in new hosts starting in August.

While new host growth mostly plateaued thereafter, a drop-off in new detections is not necessarily an indicator that operations are abating. More likely, it reflects that many previously registered domains remain active, and that operators may have shifted their focus to maintaining existing infrastructure rather than expanding it. Based on data from Recorded Future® Web Scans, approximately 40% of suspect websites in this cluster observed prior to October 17, 2026, remain active.

Title: GhostFrame: A new ESXi Implant Linked to Settra Ransomware
Context: Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access
Full Text:
Implant Deployment and Persistence

GhostFrame includes an integrated builder that generates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. The interface provides operators with deployment instructions, including compiling the binary, manually disabling the ESXi firewall, and executing the implant from a datastore. Operators must already have root-level access to the ESXi host to deploy and execute the implant, as the implant does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access.

Analysis of a recovered GhostFrame Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) sample revealed that the implant establishes persistence by copying itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and modifying the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh. The modified script executes the implant and repeatedly disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly security control, which restricts the execution of unsigned binaries. These commands run approximately every five seconds, allowing the implant to disable the controls again if an administrator attempts to restore them. The implant also executes /sbin/auto-backup.sh to preserve the modified configuration across reboots. To blend into the ESXi environment, the implant appears as vmhostd, a name that resembles VMware’s legitimate vmware-hostd daemon, by modifying its process name and command-line representation.

C2 Communications and Payload Execution

GhostFrame’s implant uses a distinctive connection strategy to communicate with its C2 server. Rather than relying on a single destination port, the analyzed sample attempts simultaneous Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections across six ports: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, and 9443. The implant uses the first successful connection for C2 communications and closes the remaining connections. If no connection succeeds within thirty seconds, it retries after a randomized delay between five and twelve seconds. This behavior can produce six near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets from an infected ESXi host to the same destination IP address, providing defenders with a potentially distinctive network detection opportunity.

Once connected, the implant functions primarily as an in-memory shellcode loader. It receives machine code from the C2 server, allocates executable memory, and executes the received payload without writing it to disk. If executable memory cannot be allocated, the implant can instead establish a conventional /bin/sh reverse shell.

Post-Exploitation Capabilities

In addition to maintaining access to the hypervisor, GhostFrame allows operators to interact directly with the VMs hosted on the compromised ESXi system. GhostFrame can enumerate registered VMs, display their names and power states, manipulate VM power states, and create or delete snapshots. It also supports enabling Virtual Network Computing (VNC) access to individual VMs and relaying graphical sessions through the GhostFrame C2 infrastructure to the management panel. This allows operators to interact with the guest VMs without establishing a separate direct connection to the guest system.

GhostFrame can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client through an operator-controlled tunnel, allowing direct access to the hypervisor’s management interface from the GhostFrame panel.

For network pivots, GhostFrame includes a SOCKS5 proxy component named gfsox. Once gfsox is deployed to a compromised ESXi host, this component allows operators to route network traffic through the hypervisor, potentially reaching internal systems and services that are otherwise inaccessible from the internet.

One of GhostFrame’s more significant capabilities is its integration of multiple credential-access mechanisms. Analysis of the frontend revealed a component named sdkmon, which the interface describes as a credential interceptor. According to the frontend, the component can modify the ESXi service configuration and intercept authentication traffic, allowing it to capture usernames and passwords from subsequent ESXi logins.

GhostFrame also integrates VMkatz, an open-source credential-harvesting tool. The interface supports extracting credential data through VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, combined memory and disk analysis, or recursive scanning of all VMs on a datastore. These methods are associated with NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, Security Account Manager (SAM) and Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and credential data from NTDS.dit.

Together, these capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying conventional credential-stealing malware inside each VM.

GhostFrame’s combination of persistent hypervisor access, remote VM management, network pivoting, and credential harvesting makes it particularly relevant to ransomware and other financially motivated intrusion operations. Its observed use in activity associated with Settra ransomware provides an example of how the framework has been used in the wild.

TAG 218: From VPN To Hypervisor

Insikt Group identified GhostFrame while monitoring the operator infrastructure behind a threat activity group it designates TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware operations.

Using Recorded Future® Network Intelligence, Insikt Group observed a cluster of victim-facing servers attributed to TAG-218 targeting virtual private network (VPN) appliances across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices. Four of the targeted organizations were subsequently published on the Settra ransomware leak site.

These victim-facing servers also connect to TAG-218 tooling, including two GhostFrame C2 servers and a MeshCentral remote monitoring and management server used for persistence that was previously attributed to Settra intrusions by Huntress. On October 12, 2026, a victim Fortinet VPN appliance was observed beaconing to both GhostFrame and MeshCentral in the same period, placing GhostFrame within the TAG-218 intrusion chain.

Key trends: October 2026

PHP2Shell reporting covered confirmed honeypot shell execution, a Fragnesia chain yielding root access on 25 servers, and Potassium-associated payload attempts. Other PHP2Shell activity involved suspected preparations for a North Korean attack, which was assessed with moderate confidence as linked to the Lazarus Group. Other exploitation activity this month included Longlegs deploying Warlock ransomware; ransomware groups exploiting PAN-OS; CL-STA-0954 targeting Fortinet products for data theft; PEERSTITCH deployment; Integrity Technology Group-enabled espionage; CyberXero’s AI-assisted exploitation; and ClingSTUN deployment.

37 of the 82 vulnerabilities enabled remote code execution (RCE). Collaboration, content-management, and enterprise platforms were the most affected product type, with 12 vulnerabilities. Microsoft had the largest vendor share, with three vulnerabilities.

Insikt Group identified public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits or scanners for 37 of the 82 vulnerabilities in this report.

The most common weakness class was CWE-78 (OS Command Injection), with eight vulnerabilities, followed by CWE-287 (Improper Authentication), with seven. CWE-22 (Path Traversal) and CWE-77 (Command Injection) each affected six vulnerabilities.

10 of the 82 vulnerabilities were at least five years old, and the oldest was approximately 16 years old.

Trend analysis

PHP2Shell exploitation enables root access and internal pivoting

In October, two vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell”), drew attention from threat actors, who also chained them with CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel vulnerability known as Fragnesia. Following their disclosure, Insikt Group published multiple notes and detection rules involving PHP2Shell in October. Highlights from our coverage include:

Root access and internal pivoting: A TTP Instance detailed a campaign chaining CVE-2026-109618 (PHP) and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP) with CVE-2026-46300 (Linux kernel), also known as Fragnesia. Dream Research reported root access on 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. PHP2Shell provided initial access, and Fragnesia enabled privilege escalation. The actor deployed web shells, stole configurations, credentials, and private keys, and maintained reverse Secure Shell (SSH) tunnels to internal systems, enabling service-account password decryption and Active Directory enumeration. Domain-account creation was attempted but not confirmed.

Technical analysis and exploit development: A separate TTP Instance explained PHP2Shell’s memory-lifecycle failures enabling unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), highlighting Apache mod_php exposure and unvalidated early PoCs. Separate TTP Instances covering reports from SOCRadar and AkatsukiLegion described actor-staged exploits, prerequisite checks, and a memory-leak-to-command-execution chain.

Threat actor pre-positioning: Two other TTP Instances covered PHP2Shell tooling on an extortion actor’s staging server and CYFIRMA’s assessment of suspected North Korean preparations using 21 compromised nodes to check 216 hosts. CYFIRMA assessed a Lazarus Group connection with moderate confidence. Neither earlier shared-hosting intrusions nor attack preparations established a successful PHP2Shell compromise.

Botnet activity: A TTP Instance covering Arctic Wolf and Cisco Talos described probes and payload-download attempts associated with Potassium, a Mirai-derived botnet. In separate TTP Instances covering Linux bots reported by Joe Security and Nextron Research, Insikt Group corroborated remote-shell, evasion, and denial-of-service capabilities in the former, and PHP2Shell testing, scanning, downloads, and persistence in the latter. These findings did not confirm successful malware delivery through PHP2Shell.

Detection rule coverage: Insikt Group created Sigma rules for Linux and Windows to detect web or PHP workers spawning shells, including PowerShell, and Suricata and Snort rules for multipart session-ID and upload-progress requests. Network detection requires visible HTTP bodies. Correlate these alerts with process creation, worker errors, and outbound activity because individual matches can be benign.

Separate PHP vulnerability: A TTP Instance reported on CVE-2026-115560 (PHP), a vulnerability distinct from PHP2Shell that could enable unauthenticated RCE in applications switching session serializers while upload progress is enabled. No in-the-wild exploitation was established at the time of publication. PHP recommended disabling session upload progress pending a separate fix; the initial PHP2Shell patches did not address this vulnerability.

Title: The Shift: Rethinking the Human in the Loop
Context: Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got...
Full Text:
Ensuring that there are "humans in the loop" is the gold safety standard for making sure artificial intelligence (AI) agentic systems act safely, ethically, and legally. However, as automated processes accelerate and scale, humans lose the ability to provide meaningful oversight over machine-speed workflows. Rather than simply inserting a human into a machine process, leaders must engineer systems that enable AI agents to operate at machine speed while ensuring they act within human-authorized intent, appropriate controls, and safety and legal boundaries. This means thinking strategically about where acceleration is possible and where slowing down to human speed is necessary to avoid catastrophic risk.

The Hiring Automation “Doom Loop” Is a Warning

Hiring offers an instructive example of how humans can be sidelined by a process accelerated by unchecked automation. Machine-assisted decision-making has long been used in the hiring process to manage volume and improve fairness and efficiency. However, generative AI has made reading and writing job applications almost completely machine-dominated, leading the CEO of Greenhouse, a human resources platform, to declare that AI had created a "doom loop" in hiring. No one intended to create this doom loop, but the adoption of automation in one area led to accelerated adoption in others, ultimately sidelining humans from hiring decisions.

The hiring doom loop is driven by two mutually reinforcing trends: more applicants are applying for each position, and more companies are relying on automation to sift through the growing volume of applications. Applicants per hire tripled between 2021 and 2024, according to one survey of hiring managers, and Greenhouse reported a 412% increase in applicants per post. Applicants are almost certainly using generative AI to spin up customized applications to hundreds of jobs at once.

Meanwhile, 91% of HR departments report using AI in recruitment, and Greenhouse data shows that the number of human recruiters has dropped by over 50%. The recruiters who remain cannot meaningfully evaluate any single application at this volume, further reducing human decision-making in the hiring process. Some companies now use AI to conduct interviews, meaning applicants may not meet an actual human at the company until very late in the process, if at all.

Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got slower. More companies are lengthening probationary periods, a sign that they're increasingly unable to identify unsuitable candidates before hiring them. Many job hunters express frustration with encountering bots instead of real humans at their potential future employer. At the same time, scammers and state-sponsored cybercriminals have taken advantage of this automated landscape to advance candidates whose real objective is to steal secrets or cryptocurrency.

A few factors made hiring one of the first processes to fall victim to the doom loop. Hiring managers were early adopters of automation, using technology like keyword-based filters to parse resumes. At the same time, successful cover letters and resumes tend to follow a formula, which makes them easy to convincingly replicate with generative AI. However, there are two factors that are not unique to hiring that make it susceptible to doom loop dynamics:

Incentives for speed and scale: as competition increases, candidates are rewarded for applying to more jobs, faster.

Mutually reinforced automation: as application volume outgrew what individuals could manage, automation spread further into the hiring process. This, in turn, drives candidates to prioritize impressing the bots rather than their future human co-workers.

The hiring doom loop is a valuable case study for managing automation because it forces leaders to account for factors outside of their direct control. Instead of responding to machine volume with more automation, developers must think strategically about the intended outcomes and potential second-order effects to ensure systems remain aligned with human intent.

Title: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
Context: Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

Key Findings

AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

AtlasCore’s Telegram posts recorded approximately $10.97 million in claimed deposits across its scam offerings between May 2 and September 18, 2026, with the deposits predominantly associated with prediction markets. PolyFucked separately advertises approximately $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures rely on threat actor reporting and remain unverified.

Magnetic Team advertises more than 3,000 simulated traders across more than 5,000 markets to fabricate convincing trading activity. Its code exposes configurable withdrawal-blocking pretexts, forced-loss controls, and pools of up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. AtlasCore similarly exposes settings to force wins or losses and impose individualized withdrawal restrictions.

All three traffer teams advertise or provide AI-assisted victim support. AtlasCore and PolyFucked also supply guidance for AI-generated promotional content, including synthetic influencers and branding, respectively. Magnetic Team’s source code contains indicators of likely AI-assisted development, suggesting AI use may extend to building and maintaining the underlying fraud platforms, although that assessment remains unconfirmed.

Insikt Group identified over 100 unique domains and subdomains associated with AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team, including administrative infrastructure and scam websites likely operated by the teams or their affiliates.

Threat Analysis

AtlasCore

In August 2026, Insikt Group identified a post on a low-tier cybercriminal forum seeking affiliates to join the traffer team “AtlasCore”. The thread was first created on May 15, 2026, by the user “AtlasCore”. The affiliate program was also advertised on a top-tier cybercriminal forum by the user “AtlasCorp” on May 28, 2026. The program includes an offering for prediction markets, as well as more typical traffer scams such as cryptocurrency exchanges and casinos.

Title: Behind Japan’s Warnings of a Cyber Crisis
Context: The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved...
Full Text:
At least two features set the Q3 Japan breaches apart from other such breaches. The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved ransomware, stolen cloud credentials, and exploited web-facing systems. The second is the scale of the attacks: single incidents now routinely affect millions of user records or organizations downstream that rely on the targeted services, such as roughly 33 million records leaked from the EPARK PeakManager reservation platform in July and 6.6 million accounts from Times Car in September.

This trend has continued into Q4. On October 7, a ransomware incident affected IDCFrontier, a Japanese cloud provider, disrupting 495 companies and local governments. Almost a week later, on October 13, 2026, a data breach affected the Japanese software company Sourcenext. In this incident, an unidentified third party misused the company’s member information retrieval API to compromise 22,519,960 customer records containing personally identifiable information, including email addresses, passwords, names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employment information, and more.

Our observations complement October 2026 warnings issued by several Japanese agencies, including the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and the Innovation Platform Agency (IPA), regarding a series of cyberattacks targeting Japan-based organizations. JPCERT/CC’s notice warned of at least four consistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) linked to recent incidents:

Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in unpatched systems or misconfigurations;

Attacking internal and external APIs, sometimes using stolen API credentials;

Exploitation of CVE-2026-72898 (CVSS score 10), a SQL injection vulnerability, in the Metabase application;

The deployment of web shells contained within .war and .jsp files on internet-accessible web servers.

Later reports attributed the cyberattacks targeting Japanese company websites to artificial intelligence (AI) agents linked to activity ranging from basic website scanning to extended attack sequences that involved multiple tools and techniques.

Japan-based Macnica Security also reported a surge in cyberattacks since July 2026 involving personal information leaks from web systems. The company noted that this increase is unique to Japan compared with other countries. According to Macnica, of the 119 cases disclosed in 2026, approximately 68% were announced since July. This accounts for about 31% of the total 265 cases over a 34-month period. The company similarly observed unauthorized access through weak authentication, stolen credentials, or exploited software vulnerabilities and site-specific flaws in application design, APIs, or access controls. Macnica could not confirm the use of AI in these attacks.

Explaining the Increase in Incidents

Multiple factors are likely responsible for the recent increase in attacks affecting Japanese organizations.

High Demand in the Criminal Ecosystem for Japanese User Data: Criminals on the dark web place a premium on data from Japanese organizations due to Japan’s financial and identification requirements and its status as a wealthy, developed economy.

Widespread Use of Legacy Systems and Software: According to an April 2026 article by Money Forward, more than 60% of Japanese firms still use legacy systems, end-of-life software, and older operating systems. Such systems no longer receive security updates and official patches from vendors, leaving known flaws exposed to increasingly automated attempts to exploit them.

Operationalization of AI Tooling: While the specific models abused are not yet confirmed, commercial AI products are widely believed to have been leveraged in the recent spate of attacks against Japanese organizations, both for automating the attack sequence (such as automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation), and for reducing the barrier-to-entry historically attributed to the complexity of the Japanese language (such as through the easier drafting of convincing phishing emails in proper business Japanese). Notably, financial institutions in neighboring South Korea were recently the target of an intrusion campaign leveraging ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI penetration-testing tool attributed to a group Recorded Future refers to as TAG-217. On October 19, the Japanese cybersecurity company GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae reportedly concluded that ARTEX was used in attacks against roughly 80 Japanese companies, with 8 of those attacks occurring in the 30 days prior to its report.

New Incident Reporting Requirements: Effective October 1, 2026, Japan’s new Active Cyber Defense (ACD) Law imposes mandatory reporting requirements on designated critical infrastructure operators. This is unlikely to account for the surge in reported incidents due to the law’s implementation date in Q4 2026, but it does imply that we will very likely continue to observe a higher volume of incident disclosures from Japanese organizations going forward, and the impending implementation of the law may have induced some organizations to disclose incidents in Q3 that would otherwise have gone unreported.

Recommendations

Insikt Group recommends that Japanese organizations consider the following:

Migrate away from and/or update legacy systems. Outdated and unpatched devices or software (including operating systems) provide an attractive, easy vector for threat actors to compromise organizations via previously disclosed vulnerabilities and exploits. AI-enabled scanning and automated exploitation have further increased the risk to these systems. Where possible, replace end-of-life hardware and software.

Harden internet-facing systems. Secure internet-exposed hardware and services such as virtual private network (VPN) servers, web application firewalls, load balancers, small office/home office routers, IP cameras, and DVRs by patching known vulnerabilities, restricting administrative access, enabling additional logging, and disabling unnecessary services. These devices have been increasingly exploited by cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors alike over the last several years for initial access.

Strengthen API controls. Verify authorization for every API request, test whether users can access other customers’ records, restrict API key privileges, and limit bulk data retrieval.

Protect accounts against phishing. Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and train staff to be vigilant against increasingly well-crafted Japanese-language phishing messages.

Limit data exposure and prepare for disruption. Delete unnecessary personal information, restrict data export permissions, test restoration from protected backups, and establish manual alternatives for critical services such as reservations and dispatch.

Adopt privileged access management (PAM). Limit administrative and super-user accounts, providing elevated rights only on a temporary, just-in-time basis.

Use Recorded Future Threat Intelligence. Customers can proactively monitor for threat actor mentions of their organization and leaked data on dark web forums, chat rooms, and ransomware leak sites by configuring alerts on the Recorded Future Intelligence Platform, regularly ingesting Insikt Group research, and blocklisting known malicious indicators of compromise (IoCs).

Title: PHP2Shell Exploitation: Two Critical PHP Flaws Explained
Context: Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize...
Full Text:
The Latest Update

Insikt Group has published a TTP Instance for PHP2Shell covering public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, observed exploit activity, and recommended mitigations. As of 7 PM UTC on October 21, 2026:

Patch status: PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026: PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.

Exploitation status: While there are some reports of emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, the available reporting does not establish the full extent of successful exploitation or confirmed compromises (1, 2).

PoC status: Publicly available repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, although their effectiveness and relationship to the confirmed vulnerabilities vary. For example, security researcher J4ck3LSyN published two alleged PoCs but subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer UAF theory underlying their proposed exploitation sequences.

How It Started

On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP initially withheld technical details and affected versions pending coordinated disclosure, warning that the release could be accelerated if vulnerability details leaked or exploitation emerged.

Ahead of the scheduled release, watchTowr reported reproducing CVE-2026-109618 and assessed that both vulnerabilities could enable remote code execution (RCE). Technical information subsequently leaked before coordinated disclosure, prompting heightened concern about potential exploitation. PHP shipped the fixes on October 21, alongside a PHP Foundation post about the release, which addressed the emergency release and improvements to PHP's security processes.

The “PHP2Shell” name comes from Wiz Research, which found the flaws with Calif and OpenAI and reported them to PHP in August. Wiz’s write-up covers the discovery and root cause in depth.

The Vulnerabilities

Both CVEs are memory-safety vulnerabilities involving PHP's handling of request memory during initialization, error handling, and cleanup. According to Wiz, out-of-memory (OOM) failures and stale internal state can expose freed or partially initialized memory, potentially enabling memory disclosure, memory corruption, and remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109618: An OOM-related vulnerability involving partially initialized request memory. Wiz identified a use-after-free (UAF) in the session upload-progress unserializer and a related flaw that can disclose PHP worker memory. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.

CVE-2026-109619: A stale-state vulnerability involving PHP globals that retain references to freed request memory. Wiz identified a UAF involving fatal-error backtraces and a separate OPcache type-confusion flaw. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Drupal and WordPress.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than a particular website application. Some exploitation paths involve PHP's session upload-progress functionality, which VirusTotal notes has existed since PHP 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. Because exploitation depends on the PHP runtime, server configuration, and reachable execution paths, even websites with secure application code may be vulnerable.

PHP identified the following affected and patched versions. Older, unsupported PHP branches are not covered by these release-specific fixes and should not be presumed unaffected.

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

8.2 releases before 8.2.35

8.2.35

8.3 releases before 8.3.36

8.3.36

8.4 releases before 8.4.27

8.4.27

8.5 releases before 8.5.12

8.5.12

Reports of Active Exploitation

Following the disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, multiple sources reported exploitation activity in the wild:

Patchstack received reports of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners by 07:34 UTC on October 21, ahead of PHP's security release.

Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht reported observing early attacks targeting the vulnerabilities. Cloudflare subsequently deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections against known exploit vectors.

Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize the techniques used in observed attacks.

Public Proof-of-Concept Exploits

Numerous public GitHub repositories have emerged around PHP2Shell, including projects advertising proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, vulnerability-testing tools, and defensive resources. Several claim to target CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 through memory-corruption techniques intended to crash vulnerable servers or achieve remote code execution (RCE). However, some rely on invalidated exploitation theories, and the existence of publicly available code does not establish that it successfully exploits either vulnerability.

Insikt Group's TTP Instance examines two PoC scripts published by security researcher J4ck3LSyN:

poc0_109618.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109618 through PHP's session upload-progress functionality, using a proposed memory-corruption technique to execute commands on a vulnerable server.

poc1_109619.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109619 through a related technique involving successive chunks of an uploaded file, similarly attempting to achieve remote code execution.

J4ck3LSyN subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer vulnerability theory underlying these proposed exploitation techniques but separately reported reproducing another memory-safety issue without demonstrating RCE.

Other publicly available repositories advertise PHP2Shell exploits, vulnerability-testing scripts, and demonstration environments. Some continue to describe the invalidated cached-pointer technique, while others claim to use different exploitation methods. At the time of this publication, Insikt Group has not independently tested J4ck3LSyN’s PoCs or other publicly available PoCs for accuracy or effectiveness.

Scale and Exposure

Two independent internet scans show how much PHP is exposed, but they count differently. Modat counts PHP services that report a readable version and were seen in the 10 days before October 20. VirusTotal counts IP addresses as of October 21, including PHP servers it identifies through signals other than a version string, such as the application, session cookies, and framework headers.

Modat: 4,384,302 PHP services on 1,886,612 unique hosts. About 79% of services with a readable version run a branch PHP no longer supports, and PHP 7.4, end of life since 2022, accounts for 878,761 services, more than any supported branch.

VirusTotal: About 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, of which only about 1.1 million disclose a version, so roughly four in five hide it. Among those that disclose their version, about 758,000 run an end-of-life branch from 5.4 to 8.1, compared with about 272,000 on a supported branch, and PHP 7.4 alone accounts for about 187,000.

Neither scan counts confirmed vulnerable hosts, but both point the same way: most exposed PHP runs on end-of-life branches that will not receive an official fix. Scans that rely on version strings miss most of the exposed surface, and running the latest release was no protection: VirusTotal counted about 85,000 IP addresses on the September 24 releases, the newest available before the fix.

Why This Matters

Millions of servers could be exposed: VirusTotal identified approximately 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, highlighting the potentially widespread reach of these vulnerabilities.

Even secure PHP applications are at risk: The flaws can allow unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, even when the application running on top of it has no vulnerabilities.

Secrets can leak without code execution: Wiz showed that the memory disclosure flaw can expose passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests.

The patch window collapsed: Details leaked hours before the release, and security researchers reported exploitation attempts before fixed versions were available (1, 2).

Many servers run outdated PHP versions: VirusTotal found that most PHP servers disclosing their versions were running end-of-life branches that no longer receive regular upstream security updates.

Compromise can spread past the web server: VirusTotal found about 394,000 PHP hosts that also expose Secure Shell (SSH), about 233,000 that expose MySQL, and about 68,000 that expose remote desktop protocol (RDP).

Logs may show little: Exploitation happens below the application layer, so application logs may record limited context.

Timeline of Events

The disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities unfolded over several weeks, beginning with their discovery in August 2026 and culminating in an emergency security release on October 21, 2026. However, vulnerability details became publicly accessible ahead of the coordinated release, prompting defensive preparations and reports of exploitation activity before patches became available.

The following timeline outlines key developments associated with the discovery, coordinated disclosure, early exploitation reports, and Recorded Future's response.

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using AI-assisted research tools.

August 20, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against Drupal.

August 21, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated RCE against WordPress.

August 24, 2026: Wiz Research privately reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team, initiating the coordinated disclosure process.

September 21, 2026: The PHP security team acknowledges the vulnerability reports and begins developing coordinated fixes.

October 20, 2026: PHP announces an emergency, out-of-band security release scheduled for October 21 to address two critical vulnerabilities.

October 20, 2026: Insikt Group publishes an initial intelligence note highlighting the upcoming PHP security updates.

October 20, 2026: Recorded Future develops Attack Surface Intelligence signatures to identify potential exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

October 21, 2026, 02:29 UTC: An archive containing leaked vulnerability information was first submitted to VirusTotal.

October 21, 2026, 07:34 UTC: Patchstack reports receiving notifications of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners, several hours before the scheduled security release.

October 21, 2026, 13:52 UTC: PHP releases security updates addressing both vulnerabilities, ahead of the previously announced 14:00 UTC release time.

October 21, 2026, 17:52 UTC: Insikt Group publishes a PHP2Shell tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP) instance to support threat detection and analysis.

Notably, reports of exploitation activity emerged before the official security release, creating a brief period during which vulnerability information was circulating publicly while affected organizations lacked an official patch. As a result, PHP users may discover exploitation attempts that occurred prior to the official patch disclosure. Threat hunters should therefore extend their lookback period for exploitation attempts to before the vulnerability disclosures were published.

Recorded Future Independent Analysis

Recorded Future's Insikt Group analyzed the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, reported exploitation activity, and defensive measures. The resulting TTP Instance provides defenders with technical context and actionable guidance to help assess exposure, prioritize remediation, and identify potential attacks.

Public PoCs: Multiple publicly available GitHub repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits targeting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These PoCs focus on exploiting PHP memory-safety flaws to achieve remote code execution, though their effectiveness varies, and some rely on exploitation techniques that were subsequently invalidated.

Exploit activity: Security vendors have reported emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, although the extent of successful exploitation remains unclear, and confirmed indicators of compromise (IoCs) remain limited. Insikt Group’s TTP Instance includes potential warning signs that defenders can monitor, such as unusual web requests, PHP errors, and suspicious server activity.

What You Need to Do Now

Organizations operating PHP-based applications should prioritize patching vulnerable systems, assessing their exposure, and monitoring for potential exploitation. Given reports of exploitation activity ahead of the coordinated security release, organizations should also investigate whether affected systems may have been compromised before patches became available.

Insikt Group recommends the following measures to mitigate the risks associated with PHP2Shell:

Prioritize Patching and Remediation: Upgrade affected PHP deployments to the appropriate patched versions, prioritizing internet-facing applications and critical infrastructure. Organizations running unsupported PHP versions should migrate to supported releases or obtain vendor-maintained security fixes. Ensure that remediation includes PHP components embedded in third-party applications, containers, and managed services.

Identify Exposed Assets and Validate Remediation: Inventory PHP deployments across organizational environments and assess exposure based on internet accessibility, configuration, and business criticality. Recorded Future customers should leverage Attack Surface Intelligence to identify potentially vulnerable internet-facing assets and validate remediation efforts.

Implement Compensating Security Controls: Where immediate patching is not feasible, restrict external access to vulnerable systems and implement applicable WAF protections, request filtering, and PHP configuration hardening. Ensure that origin servers cannot be accessed directly to bypass perimeter defenses. These measures may reduce exposure to certain exploitation techniques, but should not be considered substitutes for patching.

Monitor for Exploitation and Investigate Potential Compromise: Review web server, application, and endpoint telemetry for anomalous HTTP requests, PHP process failures, unexpected command execution, and other indicators of malicious activity. Prioritize reviewing activity beginning October 20, 2026, and investigate potentially compromised systems. Where compromise is identified, initiate incident response procedures and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Recorded Future customers can access the Insikt Group PHP2Shell TTP Instance, Validated Intelligence Event, and Vulnerability Intelligence Cards® for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the Recorded Future Intelligence Operations Platform. Recorded Future will continue to monitor developments related to PHP2Shell and provide updated intelligence as additional information becomes available.

Title: TAG-217 Targets South Korean Financial Services with ARTEX
Context: The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026,...
Full Text:
The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026, weeks before the banking campaign became public, according to new research from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Subsequent public reporting indicated that the breaches exposed personal data belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions.

Insikt Group’s investigation expands the known timeline and capabilities of the actor, tracked as TAG-217. Insikt Group uncovered tools designed to steal cryptocurrency wallet files, gain greater access to Linux systems, and test weaknesses in mobile devices. The findings illustrate the “jagged edge” of AI-enabled attacks: threat actors realizing significant gains while committing basic operational security mistakes. AI helps attackers pursue more targets across more environments, but does not prevent them from making the security mistakes that allowed Recorded Future to uncover preparations and capabilities beyond the reported banking campaign. Those mistakes give defenders opportunities to identify related activity and disrupt operations.

Targeting South Korean Banks

In early October 2026, South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) disclosed that multiple financial institutions had been hit by cyberattacks. The attacks had compromised different systems and allowed unauthorized access to different data at each victim entity, with one breach exposing the personal information of an outsourced developer and another resulting in the theft of customer data. Industry sources reported that the attacks involved the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source AI penetration testing framework. The variety of targets at each financial institution likely demonstrates an advantage of AI over human operators: the ability to opportunistically test for weaknesses at scale until a valuable target is found.

On October 7, 2026, public analysis of the incident identified that the threat actor, suspected to be a Chinese speaker, used several AI tools as part of their campaign, including Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Other reports shared network infrastructure indicators used in the campaign, including a primary server running ARTEX and the use of residential proxies, likely to obfuscate the origin of the activity.

Recorded Future investigated this infrastructure to better understand the actor’s operations and tracked this activity under the designation TAG-217.

Putting Together a More Complete Timeline for TAG-217

Differentiating between agentic and human-operated attacks can be difficult, especially when skilled threat actors use AI to enhance operational effectiveness. Agentic attacks use the same tactics and techniques as human operators, though faster and at scale. In the case of TAG-217, operational security mistakes allowed Insikt Group to piece together how the threat actor used AI tools to amplify their intrusion attempts across multiple environments and to uncover earlier preparations and a broader set of capabilities than public reporting revealed.

TAG-217 routed its traffic through residential internet connections, likely to reduce the chances of detection. Recorded Future analysts used open directories within TAG-217 infrastructure to further understand its operations (Source: Recorded Future)

Title: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
Context: The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024.

However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.

Insikt Group assesses that the Kremlin’s primary objectives regarding internet restrictions are twofold: facilitating extensive surveillance of online activity to support control over the domestic information space while maintaining connectivity to the global internet, and developing national internet infrastructure under Kremlin control, enabling isolation from the global internet if the Kremlin so chooses. Efforts in support of these objectives have almost certainly provided the Kremlin with enhanced ability to control and monitor domestic online discourse.

In this environment, individuals and organizations operating in Russia are subject to increasing operational risks, including surveillance and exposure of sensitive data, challenges in conducting emergency communications, disruptions to corporate tools and digital applications, and legal risks. Entities with indirect exposure to Russia face an increased likelihood of supply-chain disruptions and sanctions violations and, over the longer term, face challenges in assessing the political and economic situation in Russia, as restrictions limit the availability of high-quality open sources.

Key Findings

The Kremlin is very likely using managed internet shutdowns across Russia to test and improve its ability to isolate the Russian internet, though technical and political limitations make it unlikely that it will achieve its objective of establishing a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term.

In the near- to medium-term, a combination of falling approval ratings for Russian President Vladimir Putin, declining public opinion amid economic strain, and ongoing Ukrainian drone strikes very likely incentivize Moscow to impose further internet restrictions, regardless of reported public dissatisfaction with some of these measures.

The Kremlin will very likely continue to pursue strategies to deter VPN use by forcing platforms to support VPN blocks and making VPN use more expensive and inconvenient, though likely avoiding direct punitive measures against individual users.

Kremlin Systematically Tightening Internet Restrictions

Since July 2025, the Kremlin has systematically tightened access to widely used civilian communications applications and VPNs, caused regular mobile internet outages across Russia, and instituted requirements that place Russian and foreign individuals and firms under increased government surveillance. The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government to launch drone strikes against Russian critical infrastructure.

Restrictions Represent Marked Escalation in Control Over Russian Internet

Insikt Group assesses that, since 2012, Russians have seen their ability to operate without restriction on the internet decline in several waves, primarily driven by the Kremlin's calculation that Russians were using the internet to organize anti-government political actions.

2000–2012: Little Government Oversight

Laissez-Faire State Policy

During this period, the Kremlin generally viewed the internet as politically non-threatening, in part due to low internet penetration rates in Russia (from 1.8% in 2000 to 58% in 2011).

Thriving Media and Social Platforms

Individual expression on the internet was relatively free, with independent news sites such as Lenta, Novaya Gazeta, Ekho Moskvy, and Gazeta able to operate largely without government interference.

In addition, platforms such as LiveJournal and VKontakte (VK) –– Russia’s Facebook mirror –– operated largely without government control.

Minimal Government Regulation

Russian state telecommunications regulator Roskomnadzor was founded in 2008, but primarily handled telecommunications licensing rather than censorship or content filtering.

2012–2015: Blocklists and Platform Takeovers Following Mass Protests

Laws Passed Creating Blocklists of Websites

In 2012, following the largest protests in Russia since the fall of the Soviet Union, the Kremlin passed law No. 139-FZ, titled “On Introducing Amendments to the Law on Protection of Children from Information Harmful to Their Health and Development,” which created the Unified Register of Banned Websites. This introduced internet service provider (ISP)-level technical infrastructure, enabling the Russian government to block domains and IP addresses through domain name system (DNS) tampering.In 2014, the Kremlin passed the Lugovoy Law (No. 398-FZ), allowing for extrajudicial blocking of websites the government considered “extreme” or which called for unauthorized protests.

Platform Takeovers by the Kremlin

The Russian Government started taking over platforms it considered politically threatening. For example, VKontakte founder Pavel Durov was forced out of Russia in 2014 after refusing to hand over data to the Federal Security Service (FSB). The Kremlin facilitated the transfer of control of VK to state-aligned businessmen, including Vladimir Kiriyenko, who is currently VK's CEO.

Data Localization Targeting Foreign Internet Companies

In 2014, the Russian government passed the Data Localization Law (No. 242-FZ), mandating that foreign internet companies store Russian citizens’ personal data on physical servers inside Russia, likely to make it easier for the Kremlin to access that data for surveillance purposes.

2016–2021: Surveillance Mandates and Attempts to Block Platforms

Laws Passed to Mandate Data Sharing, Restrict VPNs, and Pursue Sovereign Internet

In 2016, the Kremlin passed the Yarovaya Law (No. 374-FZ and No. 375-FZ), which forced ISPs and communication providers to retain metadata for up to three years and message and audio content for six months, and to provide that information to Russian security services without a warrant.In 2017, the Kremlin passed the Anonymizers Law (No. 276-FZ), formally prohibiting the use of VPNs to circumvent blocked websites.In 2019, the Kremlin passed the Sovereign Internet Law (No. 90-FZ), which required Russian ISPs to install TSPU (technical means of counteracting threats, технические средства противодействия угрозам) controlled by Roskomnadzor, thereby giving the state the power to throttle or sever external traffic to a platform.

Attempts to Block Platforms Have Mixed Results

In 2018, Roskomnadzor attempted to block Telegram by IP-banning millions of cloud servers. The attempt failed, disrupting banking and retail systems without shutting down Telegram.In 2021, the Kremlin launched its first large-scale deployment of TSPU –– deep packet inspection (DPI) hardware –– to throttle a mainstream social media platform, thereby demonstrating technical maturity in the Kremlin’s ability to throttle platforms.

2022–2024: Crackdown on Independent Media, VPN Blocks

Mass Blocking and Shutdown of Independent Media

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin blocked hundreds of independent news outlets (including Meduza, BBC, Radio Free Europe, and Ekho Moskvy) by pushing DNS and SNI (Server Name Indication)-level blocks to TSPU devices across all ISPs simultaneously. In addition, the Kremlin throttled, before outright blocking access to, social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. This was accomplished via TSPU's packet-dropping mechanism before full blocks were applied in March 2022.

In 2024, Roskomnadzor began throttling YouTube to near-unusable levels, likely to force users onto state-controlled video platforms.

Anti-VPN Actions

In 2023–2024, Roskomnadzor began blocking underlying VPN protocols, including OpenVPN, WireGuard, and Shadowsocks, via DPI hardware.

In 2024, the VPN Advertising Ban (No. 406-FZ) took effect, prohibiting the advertising of VPNs and other tools that circumvent blocks on certain websites and platforms.

Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, which supports digital forestry management, environmental monitoring, and ecological restoration. Additional targeting involved Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers within the Caspian Sea basin. Although its geographic location alone does not establish a water-related collection objective, earlier reporting linked TAG-193 to the targeting of water-resource organizations across Central Asia, providing further context for this apparent interest.

In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. The Aral Sea disaster illustrates the lasting economic, environmental, and public-health consequences of water mismanagement, helping explain why water security remains a strategic priority.

Trusted Accounts and Services Support Access

TAG-193 frequently sends spearphishing emails from compromised government accounts, using official-looking documents to make its communications credible. Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery. While not independently establishing successful compromises of the organizations these documents reference, they do indicate targeting interests.
